items.item: Every dashboard agreeing a reading is stable is a claim about the dashboard's own rules, not about the sensor — a check nobody wrote yet can't call anything stable or broken.

at.step: Hook: one exact reading for hours, and every chart calls it stable

items.item: A value can be perfectly plausible and still be wrong — the tell isn't what the value is, it's that the value stopped doing the one thing a real signal always does.

items.item: A spike detector that isn't robust to the spike itself is checking the wrong neighborhood — exclude the candidate point before you compute what's normal around it.

items.item: The honest answer isn't that a flagged point is always safe to discard or always worth keeping — it's that you can't know which, until someone needs the record it would have been.

items.item: A rule built to catch one point at a time will never catch a fault that moves every point by the same amount — the fix isn't a stricter version of the same rule, it's a different question.

items.item: Two timestamps that should never disagree are worth more than one that's merely late — the disagreement, not the lateness, is what tells a backfill from a broken clock.

items.item: A quarantine table isn't a softer delete — it's a second, separate claim about a point that leaves the original claim completely intact.

items.item: A detection system that's merely accurate isn't done — it also has to run faster than the data it's checking arrives, or accuracy never gets the chance to matter.
